title: The oldest Marian prayer
hook: Sub tuum praesidium, found on an ancient papyrus: we fly to thy protection

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Memorare: a prayer that opens by reminding. Your line was never was it known.

A scrap of papyrus, written in Greek, torn at the edges, with only parts of its lines left. Someone wrote a few words of prayer on it, and when scholars pieced them together, they matched a prayer the Church still says. In Latin it begins Sub tuum praesidium; in the traditional English, we fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God. No grand liturgy around it. No author's name. Just a handful of people, it seems, in some kind of trouble, running toward a mother.
screen: `A SCRAP OF PAPYRUS, IN GREEK.` → `SUB TUUM PRAESIDIUM.` → `PEOPLE RUNNING TOWARD A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the nickname, and its question mark. People call this the oldest Marian prayer. Scholars argue about how old the papyrus is, and the argument isn't settled, so it's fair to hold the nickname loosely. What nobody needs to argue about is what the prayer says. Second, the picture. We fly to thy protection: fly here means flee, run for cover. It's the posture of the psalm about God's shelter, which in the Douay-Rheims says, "under his wings thou shalt trust." The prayer doesn't stand up straight and make a speech. It ducks under cover. Third, the name it calls her: Holy Mother of God, the first of the four teachings that opened this stretch on Mary. Here it isn't an argument in a council or a line in a creed. It's what people shout when they're running. Fourth, the word we. The prayer never says I. Despise not our petitions in our necessities, it goes on, but deliver us always from all dangers, O glorious and blessed Virgin. A group of people with real needs and real dangers, praying together. And it's still said: in Latin in the West, and in Greek and other languages in Eastern churches, at evening prayer and at the end of the rosary. Short enough for one breath. Old enough that its own age is a question. And plural, so whoever says it today says it with everyone who ever ran for the same shelter.
screen: `A NICKNAME WITH A QUESTION MARK.` · `FLY MEANS RUN FOR COVER.` · `HOLY MOTHER OF GOD.` · `IT NEVER SAYS I. IT SAYS WE.` · then, large: `UNDER HIS WINGS THOU SHALT TRUST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a few people in danger or need right now, someone sick, someone in a war zone, someone who can't pay the rent, and gather them into one small group, the way the prayer says we. If you pray, say the Sub tuum praesidium once, slowly, for all of you together: we fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God. If you don't, hold that group in mind as if you were all under one roof in a storm.
The oldest Marian prayer. The nickname of the Sub tuum praesidium, found on a Greek papyrus: we fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God.
Your line: we fly to thee. Never I, always we. That's today, done.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Sub tuum praesidium in Latin or English, sometimes at the end of the rosary or of Night Prayer, and Eastern Christians sing it in their own languages at evening services.

chat.says: Is the Sub tuum praesidium really the oldest prayer to Mary?
options: That's its nickname; scholars still argue about the papyrus's age, so it's fair to hold it loosely.
Yes, the Church dates it exactly to the year Mary died, so no prayer to her is older.
No, a medieval monk first wrote it in Latin, and the Greek version came much later.

notes: The index title is a superlative ('The oldest Marian prayer'); the voice treats it as a nickname and says scholars argue about the papyrus's age. The usual identification is John Rylands Library Papyrus 470 (Manchester), with dates proposed from the 3rd to the 4th century or later; the script names neither the library nor a date. Confirm.
Hook: 'torn at the edges, with only parts of its lines left' describes the fragment's state; confirm. 'Scholars pieced them together' is general.

The traditional English ('We fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God; despise not our petitions in our necessities, but deliver us always from all dangers, O glorious and blessed Virgin') is recited without quotation marks; its translation is not on the validator's list. Confirm.
Claim that the prayer is used in Latin in the West and in Greek and other languages in Eastern churches, at evening prayer and the end of the rosary: confirm phrasing.
Confirm Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of Psalm 90:4 ('He will overshadow thee with his shoulders: and under his wings thou shalt trust.').
